versions.text:
Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she asked Theo to get his teammates to shout less, then moved their work to the far corner of the park, right against the fairground fence. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, watched one recall and told Mara to keep her hands still at her sides. Just before calling, Mara's right hand had been lifting an inch.

That inch explained something the shelter staff had told her in April. Before Rook was surrendered, he had lived for two years with a man who called him all day in the same flat, bored pitch but waved an arm only when he truly wanted the dog to come. Rook had learned to tune out the voice and watch for the hand. All summer he had been reading Mara's.

On the morning of the trial, the loudspeaker crackled overhead just as Mara gave the stay command softly and walked away, but she kept her hands flat against her jeans, and Rook sat like a stone until she called. The judge awarded Rook a green ribbon. On the way to the car, Theo, still carrying the liver treats, asked what she planned to do with it. "I'm pinning it on Mrs. Ostrander's board at the shelter, because she saw the one thing I was doing wrong when I couldn't see it myself."

Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she began clasping her hands behind her back before every recall. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, sniffed Mara's jacket and told her to leave the liver treats at home. Rook had been coming early for the pocket, not for her.

So for the next two weeks Mara emptied her pockets before every session, and they worked at the empty end of the pitch after Theo's team had gone home. On the first evening Rook broke twice. By the fourth he held every stay, and by the end of the second week he would sit across the grass and wait while Mara counted to sixty.

At the trial, Rook held his sit while the loudspeaker announced the next class, and Mara gave the stay command softly and walked to the far side of the ring. Then, behind the rope, Theo tore open the bag of liver treats he had brought for afterward, and Rook went straight for the sound. The judge scored the recall a zero, and they left without a ribbon. In the parking lot, Theo asked whether they could still stay for the fireworks. "You ripped that bag open right behind the rope, Theo, after I asked you twice to leave it in the car."

Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she emptied the liver treats out of her jacket and left them in the car. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, watched one recall and told Mara to give the command more softly. Mara had been barking "Stay!" so hard that Rook seemed to take it as the start of a game. Within days of the change he was holding every stay.

On the last practice evening, Theo was bouncing a tennis ball off the fence, and between one lazy pitch and the next, Mara asked him for a favor at the fair. He was to carry the old gray blanket and keep it by the car, ready to drape over Rook's crate the minute the fireworks began. Rook had never heard fireworks, and the fair always closed with an hour of them.

At the trial, the loudspeaker boomed out class numbers while Mara gave the stay command in a near whisper, kept one hand low against her leg, and walked away. Rook held until she called, and the judge awarded him a green ribbon. As they packed up, Theo asked whether they could watch the fireworks from the grandstand. "Let's get Rook into his covered crate in the car before the first one goes off, because one loud bang tonight could undo his whole summer."

Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she began giving the command softly, almost under her breath. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, saw him jump at a slammed door and told Mara to practise during the loudspeaker tests. So each afternoon they crossed the road and worked beside the fairground barns, and within two weeks the squeals barely turned his head.

Through all of it, Rook kept his old habit. After every recall he swung around and sat on both of Mara's sneakers, heavy and settled, while she fished a liver treat from her pocket. On hot days they rested in the strip of shade under the cattle barn, whose tin roof came down at a steep pitch almost to the ground, and he sat on her feet there too.

At the trial, the loudspeaker blared twice during the recall, and Rook sat through both blasts until Mara lifted her hand and called him. The judge awarded him a green ribbon, and at the ring gate he sat squarely on Mara's feet again. Theo asked whether they should stop at the shelter on the way home to show everyone. Mara looked down at Rook. "The old kennel row where he first sat on my sneaker was torn down in June, and I keep picturing him in that last run by the window."

Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she moved their sessions to the lunch hour, when the fairground crew went quiet, though Theo's team was still out on the field. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, rolled a ball past him during a stay, watched him chase it, and told Mara to train right beside the soccer games. Within two weeks a ball could skid past Rook's paws without moving him.

By then Theo had made his pitch to his coach, and Rook had become the team's sideline mascot. Then, the Thursday before the trial, someone upended a whole sack of practice balls, and twenty of them went bouncing across the grass with Rook chasing every one. It took three more evenings of work to win back his stay.

At the trial, Mara gave the stay command softly, kept her hands at her sides, and walked away, and Rook held his sit through the whole recall. He came in straight and fast, then, for the finish, sat down squarely on the judge's left shoe. The judge looked down and burst out laughing, and Rook still earned a green ribbon. Theo, clutching the liver treats, asked why the spectators had cheered. Mara was grinning. "He sat right on the judge's shoe like it was his own cushion, and she laughed so hard her hat slid off!"
